meta.description: Genuinely Horace — Odes 1.11 (23 BC): “carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero.” A faithful literal translation of a line that’s chronically misread.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Seize the day, trusting as little as possible in the future'?
meta.ogDescription: It really is Horace: Odes 1.11 (23 BC), the poem that gave the world “carpe diem” — though the line is far more often misread than misattributed.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 65–8 BC · Roman lyric poet of the Augustan age
answer.sourceLine: This is a faithful literal translation of Horace, Odes 1.11.8 (23 BC): “carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero.” It is the very line that gave the world the phrase “carpe diem,” and its Horatian authorship is not in doubt — only its meaning is routinely mangled.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Literal English rendering of the closing clause

source.excerpt: … sapias, vina liques, et spatio brevi spem longam reseces. Dum loquimur, fugerit invida aetas: carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero. — “Be wise, strain the wine, and prune back long hope to a short span. While we talk, envious time will have fled: seize the day, trusting as little as possible in the future.”
trail: The Latin is Horace, Odes, Book 1, Ode 11, written 23 BC — the poem that coined “carpe diem.”
Wikisource prints the full ode; its literal translation ends “seize the day, trusting the future as little as possible.”
Wikipedia traces the phrase to this ode and notes “carpe” is a horticultural metaphor (pluck/harvest), not aggressive seizure.

Quote Investigator traces a separate live-for-the-moment line — Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.’s “the actions and passions of your time” — that is sometimes wrongly pinned on Plotinus or Herodotus, not this Horace line.
source.excerptNote: The famous two words “carpe diem” are only the first half of Horace’s clause; the rider “quam minimum credula postero” is what carries his actual point about the uncertain future.

source.rightsNote: Horace’s Odes were published in 23 BC, so the Latin original has been in the public domain for two millennia. “Seize the day, trusting as little as possible in the future” is a standard literal English rendering of the line with no single copyright claimant; any specific modern verse translation would carry its own status, though the classic Conington rendering (1863) is itself long public-domain.

author.name: Horace (Quintus Horatius Flaccus)
author.heading: About Horace
author.metaLine: 65–8 BC · Roman lyric poet under Augustus
author.bio: Quintus Horatius Flaccus, known in English as Horace, was the leading Roman lyric poet of the Augustan age. A freedman’s son who rose under the patronage of Maecenas, he gave Latin its most quoted tags — carpe diem, nunc est bibendum, aurea mediocritas — in his Odes (published 23 and 13 BC). His verse blends Epicurean and Stoic themes of mortality, moderation, and the swift flight of time.

misattribution.heading: The catch: misread, not misattributed
misattribution.intro: For once the name is right — this really is Horace. What goes wrong is almost everything about how the line is read and rendered.

items.why: Popular usage treats “carpe diem” as a call to reckless indulgence. Horace’s Epicurean point was closer to the opposite: because the future is unforeseen, act wisely and prudently today rather than gamble on tomorrow, per Wikipedia.
“Carpe” literally means to pluck or harvest — a garden metaphor for gathering ripe fruit; “seize” overstates its force, as scholar Maria Marsilio notes via Wikipedia.

The famous two words are only half of Horace’s clause. Dropping the rider “quam minimum credula postero” (trusting as little as possible in the future) is exactly what loses his meaning, which the fuller line on Wikisource preserves.

A different live-for-the-moment line — Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.’s “the actions and passions of your time” — is sometimes pinned on Plotinus or Herodotus with no evidence (a 2000s invention), not this Horace line, per Quote Investigator.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are genuinely Horace’s — Odes 1.11, 23 BC — but he meant clear-eyed prudence before an uncertain future, not carefree abandon, as the full clause on Wikisource makes plain.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Horace addresses the ode to a woman named Leuconoe, warning her not to consult astrologers about how long either of them will live. The poem’s force comes from its ending: after urging her to strain the wine and cut back on long-range hope, he lands on the two words that outlived the rest of the poem — carpe diem.

The line has become a cultural shorthand precisely because its second half fell away. Horace’s original balances mortality against moderation; the modern slogan keeps the urgency but sheds the caution, which is why the fuller translation — “trusting as little as possible in the future” — reads so differently from the bumper-sticker version.
context.pull: “While we talk, envious time will have fled.”
